# Changing How We Group Students for Maths

## A Letter to Parents and Carers

Dear Parents and Carers,

We want to explain an important change happening in maths lessons at our school, and why we believe it will help every child do better.

### What is changing?

At the moment, we put students into different maths classes based on how well they are currently doing — sometimes called "top set," "middle set," or "bottom set." This is known as **streaming**.

From next term, students will be taught in **mixed classes**, where children of all levels of ability learn maths together in the same room. This is sometimes called **mixed-attainment teaching**.

### Why are we making this change?

We know this is a big change, and we understand why some parents feel worried about it. Here is why we think it's the right move:

**1. Sets don't stay fixed — but they often feel like they do.**
Many children placed in a lower set when they are young stay there for years, even if they improve. Being told "you're in the bottom group" can make a child believe maths "isn't for them" — even when that isn't true. This can follow a child right through school.

**2. Every child deserves to be challenged.**
In the past, children in lower sets were sometimes given easier work and less encouragement to aim high. Children in top sets were sometimes pushed too hard, too fast, with pressure to keep up. Mixed classes let every child work on challenging material, with support to help them get there.

**3. The evidence supports it.**
Studies from the UK and other countries show that when schools stop streaming — especially in subjects like maths — results improve for most students, particularly those who were in lower sets. Crucially, this happens **without** holding back students who were doing well.

**4. It's fairer.**
Research also shows that children from certain backgrounds — including children from low-income families — are more likely to end up in lower sets, even when their ability is similar to children in higher sets. Mixed classes help remove this unfairness.

**5. Children learn from each other.**
When children of different strengths work together, they explain ideas to each other, ask questions, and build confidence. This helps everyone — the child doing the explaining learns the topic more deeply, and the child asking questions gets support from a classmate as well as the teacher.

### What will stay the same?

- Teachers will still make sure every child gets the right level of support and challenge — this happens *within* the class, through different tasks, questions, and small-group help.
- Children who need extra help will still get it, often with additional support from teaching assistants.
- Children who are ready for harder work will still be stretched and challenged.
- We will keep a close eye on how every child is doing, and we will talk to you if we have any concerns.

### Common Questions

**Will my child who finds maths hard just fall further behind in a mixed class?**
No — this is the opposite of what research shows. Teachers will give targeted support to children who need it, and sitting with children who understand a topic well often helps, not hinders, struggling students.

**Will my child who is good at maths be held back?**
No. Teachers plan lessons with different levels of challenge built in, so students who grasp ideas quickly will be given harder problems to work on, not asked to simply wait for others.

**Why is the school changing something that seemed to be working?**
Streaming may seem simple, but long-term evidence shows it often limits children's progress and confidence, especially for those placed in lower groups early on. We want every child to have the best chance to succeed.

**How will teachers manage such different levels in one class?**
Our teachers are being trained and supported to teach mixed classes effectively. This includes new resources, teamwork between teachers, and ongoing training throughout the year.

**Can I ask to have my child moved to a different group?**
Since there will no longer be ability-based groups, this won't apply in the same way. However, if you have any concerns about how your child is coping, please speak to their teacher — we want to work with you.

### We want to hear from you

We know change can be worrying, especially when it affects your child's education. We are holding a parents' information evening on **[date/time]** at the school, where you can ask questions and hear more about how this will work in practice.

If you can't attend, please contact **[teacher/contact name]** at **[phone/email]** — we are happy to talk this through with you individually.

Thank you for your support as we work together to give every child the best possible start in maths.

Warm regards,

**[Headteacher's name]**
[School name]
